translations.model: Then she went out and ordered her harp to be fetched. As soon as she began to play the harp, she mingled the harp's sound with a pleasant song. Then all the people began to praise her for her musical skill, and Apollonius alone remained silent. Then the king said, ‘Apollonius, now you are acting badly, because everyone praises my daughter for her musical skill, and you alone, remaining silent, criticize her.’
essential_meaning: The daughter fetches the harp and combines playing with singing.
All the listeners begin to praise her except Apollonius, who remains silent.
The king treats that silence as censure and addresses him directly.
alternatives: Art of music/musicianship for musical skill.
error_diagnoses: Do not translate hēt as she herself fetched the harp.
Do not make Apollonius join the general praise.
Swīgende is an accompanying participle; note12a explains the printed form without authorizing silent replacement in the Old English.

translations.model: Apollonius said, ‘O good king, if you allow me, I say that I perceive that your daughter has indeed chanced upon the art of music, but she has not learned it well. Order the harp to be given to me now; then you will now know what you do not yet know.’ King Arcestrates said, ‘Apollonius, I truly recognize that you are well instructed in all things.’
essential_meaning: Apollonius conditions his statement on the king's permission.
He distinguishes the daughter's encounter with music from learning it well.
He asks the king to order someone to give him the harp and promises an immediate demonstration.
The king acknowledges his broad learning.
alternatives: Have come upon/taken up music, with the supplied explanation of gefēoll on swēgcræft, for chanced upon the art of music.
You will learn what you do not yet know is defensible idiomatic English if the know contrast and immediate viewpoint remain explained.
error_diagnoses: Do not make mē the person commanded to give the harp; it is the intended recipient.
Hine refers to the masculine musical art, not a male participant.
Wāst and nāst are distinct positive/negative forms; a source-only negative form does not silently establish a full negative-knowing paradigm.
The initial ‘chanced upon’ wording follows Cook's supplied Latin explanation; no claim about innate talent is required.

translations.model: Then the king ordered the harp to be given to Apollonius. Apollonius then went out, dressed himself, set a crown on his head, took the harp in his hand, came in, and stood in such a way that the king and all those sitting around thought that he was not Apollonius but Apollo, the god of the heathens. Then stillness and silence came about inside the hall. Apollonius took his harp-pick and began to move the harp strings with skill, and mingled the harp's sound with a pleasant song. The king himself and everyone who was present cried out in a loud voice and praised him. After this Apollonius put aside the harp and performed, presenting many fine things there—something unfamiliar and unusual to the people. Every one of the things he performed pleased them all greatly.
essential_meaning: The king orders the harp given; Apollonius changes his appearance and returns with it.
The audience's identification with Apollo is reported as their thought.
Silence precedes his skilled playing and song.
The king and audience respond with praise.
He puts aside the harp and presents further unfamiliar performances.
Each performance pleases the whole audience.
alternatives: Plectrum for harp-pick, with its supplied meaning.
Pluck/set in motion for move the strings.
Acted/put on a performance for performed; the Latin note specifies comic and tragic performance more narrowly than the Old English.
Many beautiful/striking performances for many fine things, provided the contextual sense is identified.
English plural ‘which were unknown and unusual’ can express the sense, but the source's singular wæs must remain acknowledged in grammatical analysis.
error_diagnoses: Do not assert that the narrator says Apollonius actually became Apollo.
Do not translate the source nōm/genōm as different kinds of taking solely because the spellings differ.
Do not silently regularize singular ungecnāwen wæs to a plural Old English predicate.
In the final clause, ǣlc is the singular subject and him eallum the dative experiencers; do not reverse who pleases whom.
